title: How OAuth 2.0 actually works
subtitle: Letting an app into your photos without giving it your password

scenes.title: Alice hands over her password
scenes.narration: Alice wants PrintMyPhotos to print some pictures from her Google account. Years ago, the only way was to give the app her Google password.

steps.say: Alice types her real password into PrintMyPhotos.
The app logs in to her Google account, pretending to be her.
Problem one: it opens everything. The app could read her Gmail and Drive, or delete her photos.
Problem two: her secret now sits in their database. If they get hacked, it leaks.
Problem three: to cut the app off, she has to change her password, which logs out everything else too.

steps.callout: OAuth: **what may this app touch?** Not **who are you?**
steps.say: OAuth fixes this. It is about what an app may touch, here just the photos. It is not about proving who someone is.

scenes.title: Master key or valet key
scenes.narration: Some cars come with two keys. You keep the master key, and you hand the valet a weaker one.

steps.say: Both keys start the car, so the valet can do the job.
But you keep the master key. The valet only borrows the weak one, for the evening.
And it cannot open the trunk or the glove box. An OAuth token is that valet key.

scenes.title: Who plays which part
scenes.narration: OAuth gives each player a name. Here are the four, in Alice’s story and in the car story.

steps.say: The resource owner is Alice. The photos are hers.
The client is PrintMyPhotos, the app that wants in, like the valet.
The authorization server is Google’s sign-in service. It makes the keys.
The resource server is the photos API, where the photos live. That is the car.
And the access token is the valet key: a pass that opens only the photos, for a short time.

scenes.title: PKCE: make a secret, send its hash
scenes.narration: Before anything else, the app makes a secret of its own. This trick is called PKCE, said pixie. It proves later that the same app is asking.

steps.say: The app picks forty three random characters, the code verifier. It keeps this secret on the phone.
It runs that through SHA-256, a hash that cannot be run backwards, and gets thirty two bytes.
It writes those bytes as safe text that can go in a web address.
That text is the code challenge. The challenge goes out, and only the app knows what made it.

scenes.title: Step 1: send Alice to the sign-in page
scenes.narration: Now the app sends Alice’s browser to the sign-in page, with a few details in the web address. The addresses here are made up; every provider names them a little differently.

steps.say: It asks for a code, and says which app it is.
It says where to send Alice back afterwards.
The scope asks to read photos, and nothing else.
The state is a random value the app will check when Alice comes back. That stops another site from faking the return trip.
And here is the challenge, with S256 saying it was made with SHA-256.

scenes.title: From consent to tokens
scenes.narration: Here is the whole round trip, from the first hop to the app holding a token.

messages.label: PrintMyPhotos wants to view your photos
go back to /callback, with a code
hash the verifier, match the challenge

steps.say: The app sends Alice’s browser to the sign-in service, challenge and all.
Alice signs in on Google’s own page and sees what the app wants: to view her photos. She taps allow.
Alice comes back to the app with a one-time code. Not the token itself, because web addresses leak, into history and logs.
The app swaps the code for a token in a direct request, and sends the secret along.
The sign-in service hashes the secret. If it matches the challenge from before, this is the same app that asked.
Then it hands over the tokens. Alice’s password never went near the app.

scenes.title: Step 2: swap the code for tokens
scenes.narration: Here is that swap up close: the request the app sends, and the answer it gets.

steps.say: The app hands in the one-time code.
And the secret itself, the verifier. Only the app that made the challenge knows it.
Back comes an access token, the valet key.
It lasts thirty six hundred seconds, which is one hour.
And a refresh token, for getting a new key later without bothering Alice.

scenes.title: Step 3: show the token to the API
scenes.narration: Now the app asks the photos API for Alice’s pictures, and shows the token instead of a password.

steps.say: Bearer means whoever holds this token gets in, so it has to be kept safe.
The API checks the token is genuine, not expired, and allowed to read photos. Then it answers.

scenes.title: One token’s life
scenes.narration: An access token runs out on purpose. Here is what happens over its hour.

steps.say: The token starts its sixty minutes.
Half an hour in, requests still work.
At sixty minutes the API says no: four oh one, unauthorized.
The app sends its refresh token to the sign-in service and gets a fresh access token.
Alice never sees a thing. And if a token leaks, it stops working within the hour.

scenes.title: Authorization Code Flow with PKCE
scenes.narration: Let’s put the whole thing together.

steps.say: Alice says yes, on the provider’s page, to just what the app needs.
She comes back with a one-time code.
The app swaps the code and its secret for tokens.
And it shows the token to fetch the photos.

scenes.summary: The app gets a small key that runs out, never the password
bullets: The password only ever goes to Google’s own page
The scope asks for photos and nothing else
An access token stops working after an hour
Alice can cut the app off from her account page, and its tokens stop being renewed
scenes.narration: So, compared with the bad old days.

steps.say: Alice’s password only goes to Google, never to the app.
The app asks for just the photos.
Its key runs out after an hour.
And Alice can cut the app off in one click, without changing her password.
